newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW - Australian employment data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Australian employment data.

text.p: Australian employment fell 34,100 in September and the unemployment rate was 8.7 percent, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
Median forecasts had centred on a 7,500 fall in employment and an unemployment rate of 8.6 percent. A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follow:
RIC SIMES, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ROTHSCHILD AUSTRALIA:

"It was a worse than expected number. The labour market for some time has been very flat, in fact employment has hardly risen at since the end of last year and it must be very concerning for the government and the Reserve Bank. It does increase the likelihood of a further rate later this year, but I think the bank will still be looking for further evidence of where the economy is going to head next year before it makes a final decision."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"The labour market is weaker than we thought and looking forward it is not going to get better in the next six months. So nine percent (unemployment) is possible. It certainly adds to the calls for lower interest rates either to boost confidence or get business doing something."
DAVID DE GARIS, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"It looks to be weaker than the market expected ... It's bringing it (the labour market) back towards that soft trend. The CPI and wages numbers will be the key now ahead of the RBA board meeting in November and if we see the underlying inflation number below or at 2.5 percent I think we are looking at the real prospect of another rate cut, providing wages come back."
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"Well, I think today's data clearly strengthens the case for a rate cut and that's because the fall was much larger than anyone could have expected. The (1996/97) budget forecasts which are for through-the-year growth in employment of about two percent translates to monthly growth in employment of 14,000, so we're only probably doing half of that at the moment. So at least at this stage it's still early days for the whole financial year. We're clearly not on track to achieve the budget forecast for employment nor the unemployment rate decline that is expected down to 8.25 percent."

"Clearly it was a bit weaker than expected. We've been through a path where employment has surprised on the high side, with five months in a row of rises which is unusual for this series so now we've had a fall surprising on the down side. (But) we think the way the economy is panning out there aren't signs things are faltering further -- they're just not accelerating. We expect the status quo on employment for the next few months with monthly trend growth of 10,000. Clearly it will keep speculation alive for an easing, but the important numbers are the wages and inflation numbers later this month."

"All we need is a good wages number on the 24th (of October) and then there is a rate cut coming. The unemployment rate is going the wrong way. When they (the RBA) cut in July they were talking about unemployment stuck at 8.5 percent over the last year. Well, it has now gone up. It is obvious the economy is not going fast enough at this point to generate enough jobs to get the unemployment rate trending back down again. So the only question mark can be the wages numbers and with a labour market this weak I think the wages numbers will be well behaved. We have changed our forecast in the last few days to put a half a percent (rate) cut in."
TIM PFITZNER, TREASURY ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"It's well outside of range ... 14,000 (fewer jobs) is accounted for by the census workers coming out of the system, but that still leaves 20,000 .... We think it certainly puts some downside pressure on the outlook for the economy and the labour market is still pretty soft. We are still in the 60-40 world in terms of getting another rate cut. We still have to see the CPI and wages numbers."
